prompt: Explain to a non-technical marketing head what an API is, and why our team wants to offer a public API to partners.

hiddenFacts: Company: a travel-booking platform; partners are corporate travel desks and small travel agents.
Marketing head's worry if asked: partners will bypass our app and we lose the brand relationship.

expectedStructure: Simple analogy, then a precise one-line definition
Why partners and we benefit (distribution, revenue)
Risks and trade-offs (brand, support, security) and how we'd handle them

rubricHints.userFocus: Speaks to the marketing head's concerns about brand and customers.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Names the one or two partner use cases that matter most.
rubricHints.metrics: Mentions partner-sourced bookings or revenue share as the measure.
rubricHints.communication: Analogy and plain definition; no jargon left unexplained; checks understanding.

followUpSeeds.text: She says: 'So partners will just bypass our app?' How do you respond?
Explain rate limits to her in one sentence.
How would we know the API is worth the effort a year from now?
Now explain it to {variant}.

user: the CFO, who only cares about cost and revenue
a new engineer from a non-web background
constraint: you have 60 seconds in an elevator

prompt: Walk me through what happens, technically, when I scan a shop's UPI QR code and pay ₹200.

hiddenFacts: Expected components: payer app (PSP), the QR payload (payee VPA, name, amount), NPCI's UPI switch, payer's bank (debit), payee's bank (credit), UPI PIN authentication, response back to both apps, merchant notification.
Follow-up material: pending and timeout states, reversals, idempotency, why some payments show 'pending'.

expectedStructure: Sequence: scan, resolve, authenticate, debit, credit, confirm
Why it matters for a PM (success rate, latency, support tickets)

rubricHints.structure: Names actors, then a clear ordered sequence.
rubricHints.userFocus: Explains it so a shop owner and a customer could follow.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Spends time on the failure modes that matter.
rubricHints.metrics: Mentions success rate, latency or pending rate as product metrics.
rubricHints.communication: Right altitude: correct without drowning in protocol detail.

followUpSeeds.text: Money left my account but the shop didn't get it. What happened, and what does the system do?
As the PM of this app, which technical metric would you watch daily, and why?
Which failure would you fix first, and why?
Now explain the same flow for {variant}.

constraint: a payment made on a feature phone with no internet
market: a card payment on a POS machine, to compare

prompt: We want an LLM-powered support assistant in our food-delivery app. What are the key technical trade-offs, and would you build or buy?

hiddenFacts: If asked: 1.5 lakh support chats a day; 60% are 'where is my order' and refunds.
Constraints if asked: refunds above ₹500 need human approval; data must stay in India.

expectedStructure: Scope: which intents to automate first
Architecture: retrieval over order data and policies, actions (refund API) with guardrails
Trade-offs: latency, cost per chat, accuracy and hallucination, privacy, escalation
Build versus buy criteria (data residency, customisation, time to market, cost)
Evaluation and launch plan (offline eval set, shadow mode, metrics)

rubricHints.userFocus: Thinks about the customer in a failed order.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Starts with the top intents and keeps risky actions behind human approval.
rubricHints.metrics: Containment or resolution rate, CSAT, wrong-refund rate, cost per resolved chat.

followUpSeeds.text: How would you know the assistant is good enough to launch?
Which actions would you never let the model take on its own, and why?
What breaks first when traffic doubles?
Suppose {variant}. Does build versus buy change?

constraint: the budget is capped at ₹1 per chat
market: the app operates across 5 Indian languages

prompt: Explain caching to a non-technical operations head who asks why the app sometimes shows an old price.

context.setup: You're the PM for catalogue at a grocery delivery app.
hiddenFacts: Prices for 40,000 items change several times a day; the app caches product pages for 15 minutes.
Operations head is worried that customers are charged a different price from what they saw.
Caching reduces server load and keeps pages loading in under a second.
The checkout always re-validates price from the source.

expectedStructure: Why prices can be stale and what protects the customer at checkout
Trade-off and options (shorter cache, push updates)

rubricHints.userFocus: Speaks to the operations head's concern about customer trust.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Picks one fix and defends it.
rubricHints.metrics: Stale-price complaints and page load time.

commonPitfalls: Treats staleness as a bug only

followUpSeeds.text: A customer says the price changed at checkout. What do you tell them?
Which price changes are worth refreshing instantly, and which can wait?
What number would you watch to see the trade-off is right?
Now explain it to {variant}.

user: a store manager who only knows shelves and stock

prompt: Explain feature flags to a founder, and why releasing a new feature to 5% of users first is wise.

context.setup: You're a PM at an early-stage consumer startup.
hiddenFacts: The founder wants to ship a redesigned home screen to everyone on Friday.
The last redesign increased crashes on low-end phones.
Flags are managed through a tool; rollbacks take minutes.
The company has no experimentation platform yet.

expectedStructure: Benefits: safe rollout, quick rollback, experiments
Costs: complexity, flag clean-up, partial experiences

rubricHints.userFocus: Addresses the founder's urgency and risk.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Chooses the rollout steps and thresholds.
rubricHints.metrics: Crash rate, key funnel conversion; rollback threshold.

followUpSeeds.text: What would make you stop the rollout?
Which two numbers do you watch at 5%?
Which users do you pick for the first 5%?
Now explain it to {variant}.

constraint: there is no analytics for the new screen

prompt: A user sees an old wallet balance for a few seconds after paying. Explain eventual consistency to a business head, and say whether it's acceptable.

context.setup: You're the PM for wallets at a payments company.
hiddenFacts: The wallet is served from replicas that lag the primary by up to 3 seconds.
Complaints about balance mismatches are 0.3% of sessions (illustrative).
Double-spend is prevented at the primary.
A business head fears customer panic and support load.

expectedStructure: How this system produces the lag
Where it is acceptable and where it is not
Options: read from primary for balance, UI cues, caching

rubricHints.structure: Analogy, system, where it matters, options.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Picks where to pay for strong consistency.
rubricHints.metrics: Mismatch complaints, latency, cost of reading from primary.

followUpSeeds.text: Where would you insist on strong consistency?
What metric would convince you the lag is acceptable?
What happens at 10x traffic?
Now explain it to {variant}.

constraint: reading from the primary doubles database cost

prompt: How does a food-delivery app estimate the delivery time it shows you?

context.setup: You're a PM for ordering at a food-delivery app.
hiddenFacts: ETA combines restaurant prep time, rider assignment time and travel time.
Prep time is learned from past orders by restaurant and time of day.
Traffic and weather change travel time.
Customers cancel more when the ETA grows beyond 45 minutes.

expectedStructure: Why it goes wrong (busy kitchens, rider shortage)
How a PM would use or evaluate it

rubricHints.userFocus: Notes how ETA affects the customer's decision to order.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Names the biggest source of error.

followUpSeeds.text: How would you measure whether the ETA is good?
Would you show a range or one number? Why?
What happens in heavy rain?
Now explain it for {variant}.

market: a hill town with unpredictable roads

prompt: What happens technically when a million users try to book Tatkal train tickets at 10 am sharp?

context.setup: You're a PM at a ticket-booking platform.
hiddenFacts: Traffic spikes 50x for a few minutes.
Seat inventory is held by the railway's reservation system, which limits requests per second.
Booking involves login, search, passenger details, payment and confirmation.
Many users retry repeatedly.

expectedStructure: Describe the flow and the shared bottleneck
Trade-offs and PM decisions (virtual waiting room, fewer steps)

rubricHints.metrics: Booking success rate, time to confirm.

followUpSeeds.text: You can ship one change before next month. Which?
What would you measure on the day?
How do you keep it fair?
Now explain the same for {variant}.

constraint: the railway system limit cannot be raised
market: a flash sale on an e-commerce site instead

prompt: How does a UPI AutoPay mandate get created and then executed every month?

context.setup: You're the PM for recurring payments at a UPI app.
hiddenFacts: Mandates are created with customer approval, with a cap amount and frequency.
Pre-debit notifications are sent before each debit; users can pause or revoke.
Banks and NPCI process each debit as a collect-style request.
Failures are caused by insufficient balance, bank limits or revoked mandates.

expectedStructure: Actors: user, app, merchant, NPCI, banks

rubricHints.userFocus: Understands consent and fear of surprise debits.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Picks the failure mode to fix first.
rubricHints.metrics: Mandate success rate, debit success rate, revocations.

followUpSeeds.text: Which metric would you watch for a recurring-payment product?
Debits fail due to low balance. What do you do?
How do you keep users from feeling surprised?
Now explain it for {variant}.

constraint: the bank doesn't support pre-debit notifications
user: the user is an elderly person paying insurance premiums

prompt: How would a recommendation system for a short-video app work, and what would you ask the ML team?

context.setup: You're the PM for the feed at a short-video app.
hiddenFacts: Signals: watch time, likes, shares, skips, follows, content metadata.
A candidate-generation stage then a ranking stage then re-ranking for diversity.
New users and new creators lack data (cold start).
The company wants to increase retention without increasing harmful content.

expectedStructure: Trade-offs: engagement versus diversity, safety, cold start

rubricHints.userFocus: Considers creators as well as viewers.
rubricHints.metrics: Retention, watch time per user with diversity and reports as guardrails.

followUpSeeds.text: Which guardrail would you set on the model's objective?
Which objective would you optimise first?
How do new users get a good feed?
Suppose {variant}. What changes?

constraint: you cannot use watch time as a signal
market: the app is used in 10 languages

prompt: Explain hallucination in AI chatbots to a customer-care head, and what risk it poses to a bank's chat assistant.

context.setup: You're the PM for a bank's chat assistant.
hiddenFacts: The assistant answers questions about cards, fees and disputes.
It occasionally invents policy details when documents are missing.
Customers act on wrong fee information and complain.
Human agents handle the 20% of chats the bot escalates.

rubricHints.userFocus: Considers customers who act on wrong info.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Picks the highest-risk topics to restrict first.
rubricHints.metrics: Wrong-answer rate on an eval set, escalation rate.

followUpSeeds.text: Which topics would the bot never answer on its own?
How would you measure wrong answers?
What does the customer see when the bot isn't sure?
Now explain it to {variant}.

prompt: We want an ML model to predict which borrowers will default. What would you ask before building it?

context.setup: You're the PM for credit risk at a digital lender.
hiddenFacts: You have 3 years of repayment history on 8 lakh borrowers; thin-file customers are 40%.
Default is defined as 90 days past due; data labels lag by 3 months.
The model would decide approval and limits; fairness and explainability are required.
Previous rule-based approach rejects 30% of applicants.

expectedStructure: Define the decision and the target label
Trade-offs: accuracy versus explainability, approval versus default
Evaluation: precision, recall at thresholds, monitoring

rubricHints.metrics: Default rate at approval rate; monitoring drift.

followUpSeeds.text: How would you pick a decision threshold?
Which customers does the model hurt first?
How would you roll it out safely?
Suppose {variant}. What changes?

constraint: regulation requires a reason for each rejection
market: you expand to a country with no credit bureau

prompt: Our app is slow on low-end Android phones. Engineering says a native rewrite will take nine months. Do we do it?

context.setup: You're the PM for a consumer app with 60% of users on low-end Android.
hiddenFacts: The app is a hybrid app; cold start takes 6 seconds on low-end phones.
A rewrite needs 12 engineers for 9 months; incremental optimisation could cut start to 4 seconds in 6 weeks.
Slow starts correlate with lower day-7 retention.
The roadmap has two revenue features waiting.

expectedStructure: Quantify the problem and impact on retention
Options: rewrite, optimise, hybrid, lite app
Cost, time, risk and opportunity cost

rubricHints.prioritisation: Picks the cheapest effective option first.
rubricHints.metrics: Cold start time, day-7 retention by device.

followUpSeeds.text: How would you prove slow starts cause lower retention?
What would make you commit to the rewrite later?
What's the cheapest test you can run in two weeks?
Suppose {variant}. What do you decide?

prompt: For a flash sale, should payments be processed synchronously or asynchronously? What are the trade-offs?

context.setup: You're the PM for checkout at an e-commerce company.
hiddenFacts: Flash sale traffic is 20x normal for 10 minutes.
Synchronous payment holds the user on a spinner; asynchronous confirms later with a notification.
Inventory must not be oversold.
Payment gateway timeouts occur at high load.

expectedStructure: Define both options in plain words

rubricHints.metrics: Payment success rate, time to confirmation, oversell rate.

followUpSeeds.text: Which one do you pick for a sale, and what is the condition?
What do you monitor in the first 10 minutes?
What does the customer see if payment is pending?

prompt: Engineering says they need two weeks to cut the app size from 80 MB to 40 MB. Is it worth it?

context.setup: You're the PM for a consumer app growing in Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns.
hiddenFacts: Install conversion on low-storage phones is lower for large apps.
About 35% of target users have under 2 GB free storage (illustrative).
Two weeks of work delays one small feature.
Uninstalls due to storage are a common reason.

followUpSeeds.text: What is the feature you'd delay, and is it worth it?
How would you measure the benefit?
Who benefits most from the smaller app?

prompt: Should a field-sales app for rural distributors be offline-first or online-only?

context.setup: You're the PM for a field-sales app used by 5,000 sales reps.
hiddenFacts: Connectivity is poor in 40% of routes; reps visit 30 shops a day.
Offline-first needs sync, conflict handling and more testing.
Orders must be accurate against live stock and pricing.
Online-only is cheaper to build but stalls reps without a network.

expectedStructure: Clarify the field reality and users
